newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Conrail launches battle for shareholder votes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Conrail launches battle for shareholder votes.

text.p: Conrail Inc. formally launched Monday its campaign for shareholder approval of its proposed $8.5 billion merger with CSX Corp. in a vote that is expected to be close.

Conrail, in a mailing of proxy materials to its shareholders, said it would hold a shareholders meeting on Dec. 23 at 5 p.m in Philadelphia to vote on a change in the company's charter to allow the cash and stock deal to take place.
It said shareholders should reject rival bidder Norfolk Southern Corp.'s attempts to defeat the proposal. Norfolk Southern has offered $10 billion in cash for Conrail.

Conrail urged the shareholders to waive a Pennsylvania law that would require CSX, which bought 19.9 percent of Conrail last week in a cash tender offer, to pay cash for all Conrail shares once it buys a 20 percent stake.
"The merger (with CSX) is in Conrail's best interests and is the superior strategic combination for Conrail," the Philadelphia-based railroad said in its mailing.
Under its merger agreement with Conrail, CSX has agreed to pay $110 per share cash for 40 percent of Conrail's shares.

It would exchange stock for the remaining 60 percent at a rate of about 1.86 CSX shares for each Conrail share. That exchange was worth about $85.68 per Conrail share on Monday, making the total deal worth $8.5 billion.

Conrail said in the proxy materials CSX would launch a cash tender for the second, 20.1 percent stake, after Dec. 2, and a company representative later said it was intended that the second tender would close by the end of 1996.
Norfolk Southern is pursuing a rival all-cash bid of $110 per share, or $10 billion, and has urged Conrail shareholders to reject the change in the company's charter.
Norfolk Southern lost its attempt in U.S. District court last week to block CSX from closing on its initial tender offer, but has appealed its case against the merger to federal appeals court
The upcoming shareholder vote will be close, officials representing both Conrail and Norfolk Southern testified in a court hearing last week on the Norfolk Southern challenge.
Conrail board member Bradley Jones testified that unless CSX improved its offer, it risked losing the vote.
Alan Miller, of proxy solicitation firm Georgeson and Co., representing Norfolk Southern, testified that the decisive vote could come down to a few institutional shareholders.

Conrail needs a majority of votes cast to approve the charter amendment. It said in its proxy materials that if slightly more than 40 percent of all outstanding shares voted in favor of the proposal, it would probably win, due to the expectation some shares would not be voted.
CSX will have its 19.9 percent stake to vote for the charter amendment.
Based on Miller's testimony, institutional shareholders had about 65 percent of shares before the tender offer closed, and takeover stock specialists had about 20 percent.
Assuming they tendered all their shares, those stakes would have been reduced to about 51 percent and 15 percent, respectively.

Another key block of shareholder votes, stock held by an Employee Stock Ownership Plan, would be reduced to 7.8 percent from 10.6 percent because almost all of those shares were submitted in the first tender offer, Conrail said.

Conrail said a separate Employee Benefits Trust, with a 4.7 percent voting stake before the tender, will use the proceeds from the first tender to acquire shares in the open market. This would increase the trust's voting power, Conrail said.

Miller testified last week that employee stock plan and employee benefit shares would usually be voted in line with management recommendations. But some traders, noting, for example, that fewer layoffs are projected if Norfolk Southern wins, have said that may not be the case in the Conrail merger.

Some shareholders, already angered at roadbloocks placed before the Norfolk Southern bid, grumbled that the timing of the meeting late in the Christmas season would discourage participation. Presence at the meeting is not required for a shareholder vote to count.
A Conrail spokesman said in response, "We wanted to be able to have as long a solicitation period as possible while still permitting a second tender offer to close at year end."
